input.rationale: Following the verification finding one step further turned up a second source inside the same count, and it belongs to the same cause rather than to a new one: verifyLeader credits the leader with a vote unconditionally before it consults anything, so the count starts at one even when the latest configuration no longer gives the local node a vote - the window in which a leader has appended its own removal but has not yet committed it, or the case of a leader whose configuration has moved its vote elsewhere. The target is still the voter quorum and the acknowledgements are still gathered from every replication state, so the mismatch I recorded last turn has two sources, not one: peers that hold no vote, and the leader's own credit for a vote it may not hold. I am extending the saved behaviour on its existing id instead of adding a second entry, because it is one mechanism with two sources rather than two mechanisms, and I am recording the same extension on the investigation so the question covers both. Nothing else is added and no execution is spent; this is a reading-derived extension of a finding I already recorded and it takes the remaining budget rather than a turn of its own.

investigations.hypothesis: The verification target is the voter quorum, but the set the count draws on is larger than that in two ways: the leader credits itself with a vote before consulting the configuration, so a leader that the latest configuration no longer counts as a voter still starts at one, and the acknowledgements it accepts come from every entry of its replication state, which includes non-voting members, with no suffrage check in the counter. A leader that can reach only non-voters, or that no longer holds a vote itself, can therefore satisfy a verification whose target describes a majority of voters.
investigations.discriminator: Compare the set the count draws on with the set the target is computed over, checking both the initial credit and the acknowledgement loop: if either can contribute a vote that the voter set does not contain, the verification can succeed without a voter majority. The election path is the contrast, since electSelf asks voters only, and the lease check is the countermeasure, since it counts voters only. Reading settles it, so no execution is spent.

knowledge.statement: verifyLeader credits the leader with one vote before consulting any configuration and sets the target to quorumSize, which counts voters only, then registers the verification future on every entry of the leader's replication state; that state holds one entry per member of the latest configuration other than the local node, non-voting members included, because startStopReplication creates entries for all of them. Each heartbeat acknowledgement runs notifyAll, which calls vote on every registered future, and vote increments the count towards the target without checking the acknowledging member's suffrage. The count therefore draws on sources that may hold no vote twice over: the leader's own unconditional credit, which is granted even when the latest configuration no longer gives the local node a vote, and the acknowledgements of non-voting members.
knowledge.conditions: This revision, any leader whose latest configuration contains non-voting members, or whose latest configuration no longer includes the local node as a voter - the window after a leader has appended its own removal or demotion and before that entry commits - whenever VerifyLeader is called or another caller uses the verification to guard a read.

Both sources are instances of the same mismatch between the set the count draws on and the set the target is computed over, which is why the entry is extended on its existing id rather than duplicated. The saved use that relied on the narrower statement is the interpretation at operation 2cfc284531344e89a4293b449089c945, which stays valid and simply covers one of the two sources in its wording.

investigations.question: For a running cluster, does the public configuration API expose the index of the latest configuration entry, and what value does a caller actually receive from ConfigurationFuture.Index()?

investigations.question: When authority over a node is lost by Shutdown() rather than by stepping down, does an already-accepted Apply/Barrier duty (a logFuture sitting in the buffered applyCh) still have a completion path?
investigations.hypothesis: Apply and Barrier hand the caller a logFuture as soon as the send into applyCh succeeds; with BatchApplyCh the channel is buffered, so acceptance and consumption are separate events. That logFuture has no ShutdownCh, Shutdown() closes shutdownCh and sets state Shutdown without draining applyCh, and both the main loop and runFSM leave on shutdownCh, so a future left in the buffer has no producer that can respond it: Error() blocks indefinitely and the caller's timeout, which only guarded the enqueue, cannot save it. runLeader's defer responds only futures on leaderState.inflight, so it does not cover a future that was never dispatched. Confirmed by observation: accepted in state Leader, still queued and unresponded after state Shutdown.
investigations.discriminator: Occupy the main loop inside a handler (a public Restore with a caller-supplied reader that stalls on its first Read, which is the handshake), accept one Barrier future through the ordinary public path so it lands in the buffered applyCh, then call Shutdown() and observe whether the future is ever responded: a completion would defeat the suspicion and must name the responding producer, while non-completion together with the future still being queued in applyCh shows the duty was accepted and then lost. Executed: no completion; the duty stayed queued with the node in state Shutdown.

knowledge.assertion: the caller's timeout guards only the enqueue, and the returned logFuture has no ShutdownCh, so completion is unbounded once the duty is accepted

investigations.question: When a caller names a server that holds no vote as the target of an explicit leadership transfer, does the named server acquire leadership, and what happens to the sitting leader's authority?
investigations.hypothesis: LeadershipTransferToServer forwards the caller's id and address to the transfer routine, which only requires a replication state for that server, so a vote-less member is accepted as a target. On that target the TimeoutNow handler sets Candidate and the leadership-transfer flag unconditionally and the candidate loop skips pre-vote because of that flag, so the target runs a real election at term+1; but electSelf casts a self-vote only when the local server is a Voter in the latest configuration, and voters receiving a RequestVote from a member that holds no vote reject it - after already adopting the higher term. The requested transfer is therefore unachievable: the named target can never win, while its higher-term vote request deposes the sitting leader, and the caller's future is answered without error because losing leadership during a transfer is reported as success. Observed twice, on separate clusters with the same harness: target_ever_leader=false, transfer_err empty, term 2 to 4, original leader back in Leader state, and in both runs the target's term-3 campaign skipped pre-vote while the recovery election at term 4 ran one.
investigations.discriminator: Demote one real follower to a non-voter through the public API, then call LeadershipTransferToServer on that member and sample the real nodes for a bounded interval: whether the named target ever reaches Leader, which servers do lead, whether the original leader still leads at the end, the reported transfer error, and the term before and after. Executed twice with identical operands (CheckRuns 2b61659461634c04b53ec61c35541227 and cfde738278f04108b377b912cb3eb339); the control with a voter target (7224dba1ed234879b0cb1c65e5161bf7) moved leadership to the named server with a single term step.

investigations.question: Does the documented staging phase of AddVoter exist in the implementation: can a server added through the public AddVoter API be a Nonvoter or Staging member that the leader later promotes once it has caught up?
investigations.hypothesis: The public documentation for AddVoter states that the server is added as a staging server and that the leader promotes it to a voter once it is ready, and the membership design notes list catching new servers up before granting them a vote as a main goal. The implementation does not have that phase: nextConfiguration builds the AddVoter entry with Suffrage Voter outright, the separate Staging suffrage is only reachable by an explicit Promote command, and the library's own command documentation says AddStaging was actually AddVoter and is deprecated in its favour. The in-tree unit expectations agree with the implementation, expecting a Voter for a member added through AddVoter from missing, Staging or Nonvoter states, so the state the documentation describes is never entered through the public API and the promotion duty it describes is owed by nobody.
investigations.discriminator: Trace every producer of a configuration entry for AddVoter and every consumer of the Staging suffrage: if the only public path that can add a member writes Suffrage Voter and nothing in the non-test code ever issues Promote, the documented staging phase and its promotion duty do not exist, and the mismatch is decidable by reading rather than by execution. Executed by reading: the AddVoter case writes Voter, Promote is only reached by an explicit Promote command that no non-test caller issues, and the unit expectations for AddVoter match the AddStaging cases. investigations.question: Does the transport heartbeat fast path run appendEntries outside the main thread, and can that be observed as a term or leader-state change while the main loop is provably occupied?
investigations.hypothesis: raft.go marks processHeartbeat and appendEntries as main-thread-only, yet api.go installs processHeartbeat as the transport's heartbeat handler; the network transport dispatches strictly empty AppendEntries requests to it from its connection goroutine, and that request still runs appendEntries' term logic. The term path itself is not guarded against concurrent writers: the candidate path reads the current term, computes the next one and then writes it through setCurrentTerm, which persists and stores without any compare or lock around the pair, so a higher term written by the fast path in between is overwritten when the election's write lands. The node then sits at, and persists, a term it had already adopted and left, and can later accept or issue messages at terms it had already superseded.
investigations.discriminator: Hold the main loop's term write open by supplying a stable store whose write of the current term can be armed to block once, deliver one empty heartbeat with a term well above the current one on the fast path while it is held, then release and read both the in-memory term and the persisted term: a term after release lower than the term adopted during the hold witnesses a durable term regression caused by the off-thread write. Executed twice with the same operands (d5d2d6e4b4304f65ba05d1865 and f5bfa53fce5c4314a29fe898c38b8808), the control with the same hold and no heartbeat (68ee55636577494e915fce091da4d876) shows the held write alone is monotone, and a natural-timing probe with no instrumentation saw zero falls in 792 deliveries (c839d00a425a4b75b09fbfb353fc4fc8). The open question is now whether the rate rises when the window is as wide as a slow durable write rather than a couple of instructions, which the queued probe tests with a store that sleeps before applying the current-term write and no hold-open hook.

knowledge.assertion: the candidate path reads the current term, computes the next one and writes it with no guard around the pair, so a higher term written off the main thread in between is overwritten in memory and in the stable store
with no instrumented store, no fall was observed in 792 fast-path deliveries followed by immediate term samples on a single-voter node

limitations: The broader harmful-consequence gap has no deterministic in-process witness with the tools available here: it needs the off-thread store to land inside the main loop's read-modify-write of the term, which is a two-instruction window in the candidate path, and this backend runs tests without the race detector, so that consequence can be argued from the code but not witnessed in this run.

The narrower post-shutdown facet was witnessable precisely because it needs no interleaving: the handler's shutdown branch is taken before any term logic runs, so the outcome is decided by the node's state rather than by timing.

The fast path is reachable only through a transport that installs the handler; the in-memory transport used by the test facility does not, so every execution here supplies a wrapper that mirrors the network transport's classification and dispatch rather than exercising its socket path.

investigations.question: Can the log cache serve an entry value that the underlying log store no longer agrees with, for producers inside this package?
investigations.hypothesis: The cache keeps the caller's Log pointers in its ring and returns a cached entry when the slot's index matches, so its view agrees with the store only as long as nothing mutates a stored Log afterwards, or as long as the store keeps the same object rather than a copy. The in-memory store keeps the same pointers, so for that store the two views are the same objects; for a copying store, a caller that mutates a stored Log would make the cache serve the mutated value while the durable copy kept the original.
investigations.discriminator: Check every non-test producer that hands a Log to the store: if each finishes filling an entry before storing it and never mutates it afterwards, then no in-tree producer can make the cache and the store disagree, and the residual hazard is confined to external callers using a copying store. Reading settles it, so no execution is spent.

investigations.question: Does a message the node would reject as unsupported on every other RPC path still take effect when it arrives as a heartbeat on the fast path?
investigations.hypothesis: The version and header gate lives in processRPC, which every consumer-channel request passes; the fast path bypasses processRPC and calls appendEntries from processHeartbeat, where nothing inspects the header, and the transport's classification is a shape test rather than a compatibility test. A heartbeat advertising an unsupported protocol version is therefore processed, and processing it adopts a higher term, sets the node to follower and records the sender as leader.
investigations.discriminator: Compare the two delivery paths for the same request shape: if a request with an unsupported protocol version is dropped on the consumer path and processed on the fast path, the gate is bypassed on that path. Reading settles it since the gate is a single call at the top of processRPC and the fast path has no equivalent, so no execution is spent.

investigations.question: Does a leader verification establish that a majority of the voters can be reached, or can acknowledgements from members that hold no vote satisfy it?
investigations.hypothesis: The verification target is the voter quorum, but the set of possible acknowledgements is the leader's whole replication state, which includes non-voting members; nothing filters by suffrage on either side, so a leader that can reach only non-voters can satisfy the verification while a majority of voters is unreachable.
investigations.discriminator: Compare the set the votes come from with the set the target is computed over: if the acknowledgement set is strictly larger than the voter set and the counter does not filter, the verification can succeed without a voter majority; and check the same pattern on the election path, where electSelf asks only voters, to see whether the exposure is specific to verification. Reading settles it, so no execution is spent.

Acknowledgements from non-voting members therefore count towards a leader verification.

result.summary: Following the verification finding one step further turned up a second source inside the same count, and I recorded it as an extension of the same cause rather than as a new one. verifyLeader credits the leader with a vote unconditionally before it consults any configuration, and only then sets the target to the voter quorum and registers the verification on every replication state; so the count draws on sources that may hold no vote in two ways: the acknowledgements of non-voting members, which I recorded last turn, and the leader's own self-credit, which is granted even when the latest configuration no longer gives the local node a vote, the window a leader occupies after appending its own removal or demotion and before that entry commits. I extended the saved behaviour on its existing id with a changed premise that says plainly what moved - the narrower statement named one source and reading shows a second of the same kind - and recorded the same extension on the investigation so the question covers both sources, with the contrast and countermeasure kept in view: elections are unaffected because electSelf asks voters only, and the leader-lease check counts voters only and so bounds the false positive. I spent no execution on it because it is a reading-derived extension, and I chose it over another closing hand-off after the controller pointed out that the unchanged submission had already been retained. investigations.question: Does the transport heartbeat fast path run appendEntries outside the main thread, and can that be observed as a term or leader-state change while the main loop is provably occupied?
investigations.hypothesis: raft.go marks processHeartbeat and appendEntries as main-thread-only, yet api.go installs processHeartbeat as the transport's heartbeat handler; the network transport dispatches strictly empty AppendEntries requests to it from its connection goroutine, and that request still runs appendEntries' term logic. The term path itself is not guarded against concurrent writers: the candidate path reads the current term, computes the next one and then writes it through setCurrentTerm, which persists and stores without any compare or lock around the pair, so a higher term written by the fast path in between is overwritten when the election's write lands. The node then sits at, and persists, a term it had already adopted and left, and can later accept or issue messages at terms it had already superseded.
investigations.discriminator: Hold the main loop's term write open by supplying a stable store whose write of the current term can be armed to block once, deliver one empty heartbeat with a term well above the current one on the fast path while it is held, then release and read both the in-memory term and the persisted term: a term after release lower than the term adopted during the hold witnesses a durable term regression caused by the off-thread write. Executed twice with the same operands (d5d2d6e4b4304f65ba05d1865 and f5bfa53fce5c4314a29fe898c38b8808), the control with the same hold and no heartbeat (68ee55636577494e915fce091da4d876) shows the held write alone is monotone, and a natural-timing probe with no instrumentation saw zero falls in 792 deliveries (c839d00a425a4b75b09fbfb353fc4fc8). limitations: The broader harmful-consequence gap has no deterministic in-process witness with the tools available here: it needs the off-thread store to land inside the main loop's read-modify-write of the term, which is a two-instruction window in the candidate path, and this backend runs tests without the race detector, so that consequence can be argued from the code but not witnessed in this run.

The narrower post-shutdown facet was witnessable precisely because it needs no interleaving: the handler's shutdown branch is taken before any term logic runs, so the outcome is decided by the node's state rather than by timing.

investigations.question: Can the log cache serve an entry value that the underlying log store no longer agrees with, for producers inside this package?
investigations.hypothesis: The cache keeps the caller's Log pointers in its ring and returns a cached entry when the slot's index matches, so its view agrees with the store only as long as nothing mutates a stored Log afterwards, or as long as the store keeps the same object rather than a copy. The in-memory store keeps the same pointers, so for that store the two views are the same objects; for a copying store, a caller that mutates a stored Log would make the cache serve the mutated value while the durable copy kept the original.
investigations.discriminator: Check every non-test producer that hands a Log to the store: if each finishes filling an entry before storing it and never mutates it afterwards, then no in-tree producer can make the cache and the store disagree, and the residual hazard is confined to external callers using a copying store. Reading settles it, so no execution is spent.

investigations.question: Does a message the node would reject as unsupported on every other RPC path still take effect when it arrives as a heartbeat on the fast path?
investigations.hypothesis: The version and header gate lives in processRPC, which every consumer-channel request passes; the fast path bypasses processRPC and calls appendEntries from processHeartbeat, where nothing inspects the header, and the transport's classification is a shape test rather than a compatibility test. A heartbeat advertising an unsupported protocol version is therefore processed, and processing it adopts a higher term, sets the node to follower and records the sender as leader.
investigations.discriminator: Compare the two delivery paths for the same request shape: if a request with an unsupported protocol version is dropped on the consumer path and processed on the fast path, the gate is bypassed on that path. Reading settles it since the gate is a single call at the top of processRPC and the fast path has no equivalent, so no execution is spent.

investigations.question: Does a leader verification establish that a majority of the voters can be reached, or can acknowledgements from members that hold no vote satisfy it?
investigations.hypothesis: The verification target is the voter quorum, but the set the count draws on is larger than that in two ways: the leader credits itself with a vote before consulting the configuration, so a leader that the latest configuration no longer counts as a voter still starts at one, and the acknowledgements it accepts come from every entry of its replication state, which includes non-voting members, with no suffrage check in the counter. A leader that can reach only non-voters, or that no longer holds a vote itself, can therefore satisfy a verification whose target describes a majority of voters.
investigations.discriminator: Compare the set the count draws on with the set the target is computed over, checking both the initial credit and the acknowledgement loop: if either can contribute a vote that the voter set does not contain, the verification can succeed without a voter majority. The election path is the contrast, since electSelf asks voters only, and the lease check is the countermeasure, since it counts voters only. Reading settles it, so no execution is spent.

history.question: Does a leader verification establish that a majority of the voters can be reached, or can acknowledgements from members that hold no vote satisfy it?
history.hypothesis: The verification target is the voter quorum, but the set of possible acknowledgements is the leader's whole replication state, which includes non-voting members; nothing filters by suffrage on either side, so a leader that can reach only non-voters can satisfy the verification while a majority of voters is unreachable.
history.discriminator: Compare the set the votes come from with the set the target is computed over: if the acknowledgement set is strictly larger than the voter set and the counter does not filter, the verification can succeed without a voter majority; and check the same pattern on the election path, where electSelf asks only voters, to see whether the exposure is specific to verification. Reading settles it, so no execution is spent.

knowledge.statement: The network transport classifies an AppendEntries request as a heartbeat only when the term is set, a leader address is present, the previous log entry and term are zero, there are no entries and the leader commit index is zero, and it then dispatches that request synchronously to the installed handler on the connection goroutine before waiting for the response. The installed handler is Raft.processHeartbeat, which calls appendEntries; both are documented as main-thread-only, and appendEntries runs its term logic before anything about entries matters, so an empty heartbeat with a term above the node's current term calls setState(Follower) and setCurrentTerm from that goroutine. The in-memory transport's SetHeartbeatHandler is a no-op, so this path exists only for transports that implement it.
knowledge.conditions: This revision, any node whose transport implements the heartbeat fast path (for example NetworkTransport) and that has been configured through NewRaft, which installs processHeartbeat as the handler; empty heartbeats from a peer with a higher term are enough to take it.

knowledge.statement: On one real single-node Raft instance in Leader state at term 2, with its main loop provably blocked inside a handler, one empty heartbeat carrying term 3 was dispatched through a transport that installs the handler the way the network transport does and returned success, and the node's term already read 3 and its state already read Follower at the moment of sampling inside that window; both values were unchanged after the handler was released. The release path is transport-supplied: NetworkTransport's Close signals the channel its response wait selects on, InmemTransport's Close does not signal its shutdown channel at all, and Raft.Shutdown's future closes the transport only when the caller waits on it.

knowledge.statement: verifyLeader credits the leader with one vote before consulting any configuration and sets the target to quorumSize, which counts voters only, then registers the verification future on every entry of the leader's replication state; that state holds one entry per member of the latest configuration other than the local node, non-voting members included, because startStopReplication creates entries for all of them. Each heartbeat acknowledgement runs notifyAll, which calls vote on every registered future, and vote increments the count towards the target without checking the acknowledging member's suffrage. The count therefore draws on sources that may hold no vote twice over: the leader's own unconditional credit, which is granted even when the latest configuration no longer gives the local node a vote, and the acknowledgements of non-voting members.
